definition: A cluster of learning and performance changes that arise when learners encounter errors, feedback, worked examples, or simulation-based cases and then revise or fail to revise their reasoning.
description: This community captures outcomes in which learners either improve, partially improve, or do not improve after exposure to erroneous examples, solution-focused or detailed feedback, worked examples, simulation mistakes, and spaced testing with immediate feedback. The shared pattern is that these resources can trigger active sense-making, relationship construction, and richer clinical reasoning knowledge, but they can also produce superficial processing, longer learning time, or no consolidation when errors are not recognized or when demands are too high. In realist terms, the cluster represents the downstream effects of feedback- and error-rich learning conditions on diagnostic reasoning, prioritisation, and preparedness.

definition: Learners engage with repeated, guided case work that helps them compare case information, build and test illness scripts, and respond with more structured diagnostic reasoning and help-seeking.
description: This cluster captures a mechanism-response pattern in which case-based practice, prompts, and supported discussion lead learners to actively match, test, and refine their diagnostic thinking against case information. Across the studies, the response includes stronger illness-script development, faster recognition, strengthened concept links, improved SCT performance, and more confident use of structured senior-call or SBAR-style help-seeking. definition: Changes in diagnostic reasoning performance and self-monitoring that emerge when learners engage with case-based, self-explanatory, or bias-focused clinical reasoning teaching.
description: This cluster captures the outcomes of interventions that prompt students to question initial hypotheses, generate explanations to themselves, and reflect on their reasoning while working through cases. Across studies, these resources are associated with better diagnostic accuracy or error reduction in some settings, especially with less familiar cases or misleading information, but also with unchanged inference generation or no positive effect in familiar cases. The shared pattern is not simple performance gain, but calibration of reasoning: students monitor the limits of prior knowledge, stay closer to the case text, and sometimes repair misunderstandings or identify a second diagnosis.

definition: A set of teaching and practice resources that make expert diagnostic reasoning visible and organised so novices can use schema, features, and contrast to improve case-solving.
description: This cluster captures instructional arrangements such as elaborated doctor explanations, deconstructed consultations, contrastive learning, ECG examples, and schema-based or combined-reasoning instruction that expose how diagnoses are distinguished. In realist terms, these resources trigger learner responses such as understanding expert reasoning, identifying tutorial concepts, and using structured clinical features or similarity-based recognition, which then produce better immediate and delayed diagnostic performance, especially in less familiar cases. The same cluster also includes negative responses such as frustration or difficulty when the reasoning is hard to grasp, showing that the mechanism depends on whether the support is sufficiently structured for novice diagnosticians.

definition: A set of prompts, paired examples, and structured criteria that help novices notice, compare, and name diagnostic features when working with unfamiliar cases.
description: This cluster represents resources that scaffold learners’ diagnostic work by making salient features, labels, and comparisons available in a structured form. Across the studies, these supports operate by prompting feature awareness, slowing or guiding analytic responding, and helping learners compare normal and abnormal or alternative cases, which can improve discriminability and readiness to identify abnormalities. Their effect is strongest when the topic is less familiar and when the resource is actually used; perceived burden, complexity, or non-use can limit the mechanism from operating.

definition: A set of case, data, and instructional resources that help learners connect patient information to diagnostic mechanisms and reasoning processes.
description: This cluster represents resources that make diagnostic reasoning possible or easier by supplying structured cases, worked examples, vetted materials, and exposure to clinical pathology data. In realist terms, these resources operate by helping learners recognise the diagnostic value of laboratory and history data, trace abnormalities to mechanisms, and coordinate processing strategies across different expertise levels and settings such as dermatology or longitudinal diagnosis. Their significance lies in how they support learning when data are complex, poorly recorded, or potentially biased, while also shaping interest and acclimatisation to field-specific language and case formats.

definition: A set of prompts, tasks, and informational conditions that leave learners to reason without sufficient guidance, often producing variable or weak diagnostic inference.
description: This cluster represents the resource side of situations in which learners are asked to diagnose or infer under minimal direction: natural-strategy prompts, unguided task instructions, speeded first-diagnosis prompts, and self-selected strategies. Across studies, these conditions are associated with inconsistent attention to co- and invariation, uncertain strategy implementation, and frequent failure to generate stronger biomedical or analytic inferences, especially when suggestions are inaccurate or the topic is familiar. In realist terms, the resource offered is an under-specified reasoning environment, and the observed outcomes are poorer accuracy, no observable benefit, or no demonstrated learning.

definition: A learner response in which low-stakes, active testing is experienced as enjoyable or challenging and is taken up voluntarily, supporting repeated practice and longer-term retention.
description: This cluster describes how formative, credit-free, or otherwise non-incentivized testing formats can elicit a willing response from learners: they engage with repeated key-feature tests, video-based practice, or serious-game formats because the activity is enjoyable, challenging, or worth recommending and replaying. In the CMO logic, the offered resource is an active-response assessment or practice environment; the mechanism-response is voluntary uptake, revision-oriented use, and willingness to continue using it; the observed outcomes include higher long-term retention scores and stable decision pace rather than faster decisions. The cluster also includes the idea that decision speed is not the valid target here, but knowledge storage and retrieval are, especially when learners choose to revisit the material.

definition: Learners take up and use a structured reasoning approach after exposure to guided examples, prompts, and modelled consultation reasoning in clinical-reasoning tasks.
description: This cluster captures the outcome in which students and trainees adopt a more structured way of reasoning when they are supported by self-explanation prompts, model observation, strategy-guided case design, and near-peer or resident examples. Across video-enriched cases, consultation tasks, and real-patient encounters, the shared result is that learners elaborate their own ideas, relate similarities and differences, and perceive the consulting strategy as useful. The reported consequence is stronger reasoning performance, including superior far-transfer accuracy compared with control conditions.
